title: About fifteen million
hook: Jews today live mostly in Israel and North America, with communities worldwide

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rebecca Gratz, and the line sunday school: a school on the day the children were free. Did you teach a child something? That closes the women's stretch. Today we turn to Jewish life now, and start by counting. Day one thousand forty-five.

Some prayers need a minyan, a quorum, and so someone at the door has to count heads. And in some synagogues, the person counting won't say one, two, three. Some say, not one, not two, not three. Some count by the words of a verse, one word per person. It sounds like a quirk. It's actually a very old instinct: be careful about counting people like objects. Keep that instinct in mind, because today's title is a number, and an enormous one. About fifteen million.
screen: `COUNTING FOR A MINYAN.` → `NOT ONE, NOT TWO.` → `A VERY OLD CAUTION.`

segments.voice: The caution goes back to the Torah. When Moses is told to take a census, each person gives half a shekel of silver, so that no plague comes among them. The rabbis read it this way: count the coins, not the heads. Later, when King David counts the people directly, the book of Samuel tells of a plague that follows. Behind both stories sits a conviction: a person is not a unit. And there's an older promise still. God takes Abraham outside at night and says: "Look now toward heaven, and count the stars, if thou be able to count them." The point of that count is that you can't finish it. Now the modern number in today's title: about fifteen million Jews in the world. It is an estimate, not a head count, because counting Jews raises real questions. Who counts? Jewish movements answer differently. Orthodox and Conservative Judaism count a person Jewish through a Jewish mother or a conversion under Jewish law; Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism in North America also count a child of one Jewish parent who is raised Jewish. Some people with Jewish roots don't call themselves Jewish; some who do, others wouldn't count. So the number comes with an asterisk. Where do they live? Mostly in two places, Israel and North America. And then in communities around the world: France and Britain, Argentina and Brazil, Russia and Ukraine, South Africa, Australia, Morocco, India, and elsewhere, some large, some a handful of families with one old synagogue. The number is big and small at once. Big enough to fill cities. Small next to the stars. Each one of them a name, not a unit.
screen: `COUNT THE COINS, NOT THE HEADS.` · `COUNT THE STARS, IF YOU CAN.` · `WHO COUNTS? MOVEMENTS DIFFER.` · `ISRAEL, NORTH AMERICA, EVERYWHERE.` · then, large: `FIFTEEN MILLION.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: count your own community, the old careful way. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind the people who make up your community: a congregation, a family, a team, the regulars at a café, a street. Don't count them with numbers. Instead, go one by one, and give each one a name, or a face, or one thing they do. Notice who comes easily and who you almost forgot. Keep going until you run out, or until the bell. That's a count where every one is a person. The bell holds the time.
About fifteen million. An estimate of Jews in the world today, living mostly in Israel and North America, with communities worldwide, and counted, by an old instinct, with care. Today's word.
Your line: fifteen million. Today, when you hear a big number about people, picture one face inside it. Day one thousand forty-five.

howItsDone: Some communities gathering a minyan avoid counting people by number, saying "not one, not two" or counting with the words of a verse; population estimates are made by demographers, who note that the answer depends on who is counted.
